problem: Active Neural SLAM (ANS) confuses floors with similarly coloured furniture, accumulates mapping and pose errors, and revisits already explored areas because of poor long-term/short-term goal selection. End-to-end RL exploration scales poorly to large environments.
motivation: Fast and effective exploration of unseen 3D environments is a core challenge for autonomous robots, which must map and localize from camera data alone. Attention can help the agent focus on large obstacles for mapping and on unexplored regions for goal selection, which would cut wandering and mapping error.
key_idea: Insert CBAM (spatial and channel attention) into the RGB-processing ResNet18 encoders of the ANS mapper and local policy so that large obstacles and unknown-space channels are up-weighted.
insight: Combined CBAM gives only a small but consistent gain in coverage over ANS (0.953 vs 0.948 overall, 0.867 vs 0.856 in large scenes). The ablations show that neither attention alone helps: channel-only (NASca) and spatial-only (NASsa) do no better than ANS and are worse in large scenes (NASca is also slower), and only their combination improves it. The authors attribute NASca's failure to channel-weight mismatch between mapping and navigation, though this is not verified. The gains are marginal, on a single benchmark, with no significance testing.
method: SLAM module (Mapper + pose estimator): predicts an egocentric 2D obstacle map from RGB and estimates the relative pose change, then fuses the map into a global map via spatial transformation. Uses a ResNet18 conv layer with 2 CBAM modules, 2 FC layers (dropout 0.5) and 3 deconv layers; the pose estimator has 3 conv and 3 FC layers.
Spatial attention: a 7x7 conv over avg- and max-pooled features followed by a sigmoid gives a mask that up-weights large obstacles and walls over small decorations.

Channel attention: a shared MLP over avg- and max-pooled features followed by a sigmoid, applied to the 4-channel Global Policy input (map, pose, visited), intended to prioritise unknown-space channels.
CBAM integration: CBAM is added after the first and last conv layers of a pre-trained ResNet18, leaving its blocks untouched so pre-trained weights are reused.
Global Policy: a PPO policy (5 conv + 3 FC) takes the map, pose and visited-region channels and outputs a long-term goal.
Path planning: FMM computes the shortest path on the current obstacle map to the long-term goal, and the point 0.25 m along it is the short-term goal; unexplored areas are treated as free.
Local Policy: a ResNet18 + 2 CBAM + FC + GRU policy maps RGB and the short-term goal to low-level actions.

setting.backbone: ResNet18 (ImageNet pre-trained) + CBAM, GRU local policy, PPO global policy (trained/fine-tuned)
setting.training_data: Gibson training scenes (72 indoor scenes) in Habitat; no extra data
setting.observation: egocentric RGB with noisy sensor pose readings
setting.action_space: low-level discrete actions from the local policy toward FMM short-term goals

numbers.extra: Metric is coverage (exploration), not success; Cov in m2; text also cites 31.981 m2 as the NAS overall Cov, which differs from the table's 32.034
numbers.evidence: Table 2 The results of all modes, NAS row

numbers_note: Results are reported as exploration coverage (%Cov, Cov in m2), not navigation SR/SPL, even though the text calls the metric SPL. There are inconsistencies between text and table (e.g. ANS 32.701 vs 31.739 m2; NAS 31.981 vs 32.034). Runtimes over 71 episodes: ANS 5h35m20s, NASca 6h25m53s, NASsa 4h37m13s, NAS 5h30m7s.
results: NAS reaches 0.953 relative coverage vs ANS 0.948 overall (+0.5%) and 0.867 vs 0.856 in large scenes (+1.1%), and the authors report about 20% relative coverage gain over ANS at 300-600 steps in large environments. It is well above the end-to-end RL baselines (0.737-0.789) and its runtime is comparable to ANS (5h30m vs 5h35m).
limitations: Improvements over ANS are tiny (0.5% overall) with no variance or significance analysis, and text and table numbers are inconsistent
Evaluated only in Habitat/Gibson with coverage metrics; no real robot and no goal-conditioned navigation success metrics
Single-attention variants do not help or are slower, and the explanation (channel weight mismatch) is speculative
